items.title: Synthesizing Graph Queries from Demonstrations
items.abstract: Writing graph queries is challenging for non-experts due to the complexity of graph data models and the need to identify proper graph patterns. While recent research has advanced query synthesis for relational and document databases, the problem of synthesizing graph queries remains under-explored. We present a novel approach for synthesizing graph queries from computation demonstrations, where users specify the desired output through expressions over properties of input graphs. Our method addresses the challenge of inferring meaningful graph patterns for matching and efficiently constructing the remaining components of the query. Specifically, we combine graph mining, which identifies candidate patterns across input graphs, with deduction-based pruning, which guides an efficient synthesis of the filtering predicate and return clause. We have implemented our approach in a tool called DMiner and evaluated it on 90 benchmarks. Experimental results show that DMiner successfully synthesizes desired queries for 87 benchmarks, with an average synthesis time of 0.6 seconds per query. This outperforms both enumerative search and LLM baselines. We also conducted a user study, which shows that users can provide demonstrations with modest effort and 87.5% of the provided demonstrations are sufficient for DMiner to synthesize the desired query.

items.title: Teachers' Navigation of Assessing Written Work in Times of Generative AI
items.abstract: Teachers’ assessment practices are changing as generative artificial intelligence (genAI) becomes embedded in students’ schoolwork. While existing research has highlighted teachers’ concerns about AI use in written assignments, assessment practices have received limited analytical attention. This exploratory qualitative study investigates how teachers reason about assessment practices in genAI-rich contexts and examines the adequacy of the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework for understanding these practices. Drawing on survey responses and interviews from licensed Swedish secondary school teachers, the reflexive thematic analysis reveals that assessment emerges as the central practice through which teachers renegotiate what counts as knowledge and how assessment judgements can be legitimised. Teachers describe assessment as epistemically uncertain and reliant on professional judgement, while also raising concerns about equity and legal certainty. The study suggests that assessment constitutes an integrative dimension of teachers’ professional knowledge and proposes extending TPACK to include an explicit assessment dimension (TPACK-A).

items.title: Technology and Economic Transformation in Sri Lanka
items.abstract: This research paper examines the role of technology in supporting economic transformation and sustainable economic growth in Sri Lanka. The study investigates how information and communication technology (ICT), digital technologies, cloud computing, data analytics, artificial intelligence, automation and other emerging technologies can contribute to productivity improvement, export diversification, foreign-exchange generation, employment and regional economic development.The study uses secondary data and evidence from official and institutional sources, including the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, World Bank, Information and Communication Technology Agency of Sri Lanka, Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority and the Food and Agriculture Organization. The research compares selected traditional and technology-enabled economic activities and examines opportunities for applying technology to agriculture, tourism, manufacturing and services.The findings indicate that technology should not be considered only as a separate IT industry. Instead, digital technologies can be integrated into existing sectors such as agriculture, apparel, tourism, manufacturing, logistics and financial services while simultaneously expanding technology-enabled exports. The paper proposes a technology-led economic development framework based on digital infrastructure, human capital, sectoral technology adoption, digital exports and regional inclusion.The study is based on secondary data and provides a descriptive analysis rather than a causal econometric assessment. It identifies opportunities and constraints and proposes directions for future research and technology-driven economic development in Sri Lanka.

items.title: Technology Focus: Artificial Lift (October 2026)
items.abstract: _ The next phase of digital transformation in oil and gas is being shaped by a new generation of artificial-intelligence (AI) systems that combine engineering physics with machine learning (ML). Unlike traditional AI approaches that rely primarily on historical data, physics-based AI integrates physical laws, engineering expertise, and operational constraints directly into the learning process. Three recent SPE papers illustrate how this paradigm is transforming the industry through intelligent condition monitoring, virtual sensing, and autonomous production optimization. Paper SPE 229219 addresses one of the more fundamental challenges in industrial AI: the scarcity of labeled failure data. Equipment failures are infrequent, yet ML models require large numbers of labeled examples to perform reliably. The authors overcome this limitation by using physics-based rules to identify potential failure events from historical electrical-submersible-pump sensor data. These rules generate ML labels, turning decades of engineering experience into training data. By converting physical understanding into digital intelligence, the framework enables AI systems to learn meaningful patterns even with limited failure examples. This represents a significant advancement because it shifts physics from a validation tool to an active source of knowledge generation. While the first paper focuses on knowledge creation, paper SPE 233457 focuses on visibility. Production optimization depends on accurate measurements, yet many wells operate with limited instrumentation or unreliable flow measurements. The authors address this challenge through a hybrid physics/ML virtual flowmetering framework that combines flow physics, well-performance relationships, and ML models. The resulting system functions as a virtual sensor, estimating production behavior without requiring extensive physical measurement infrastructure. This capability is strategically important because it lets operators expand surveillance coverage across large-asset portfolios while reducing dependence on costly instrumentation. The study demonstrates that physics-based AI can provide operational visibility in environments where direct measurement is impractical or unavailable. The third paper, SPE 230130, illustrates the evolution from insight to action. The authors describe an AI-enabled autonomous gas lift optimization system that integrates physics-based models, inferential sensors, ML, and digital-twin technologies. Unlike conventional optimization workflows that rely heavily on manual engineering intervention, the system continuously evaluates production conditions and dynamically adjusts operating parameters. Physics provides the operational boundaries and engineering constraints that allow AI to optimize production safely and reliably. This work demonstrates how physics-based AI can move beyond monitoring and prediction to become an active participant in operational decision-making. Together, these papers reveal a powerful industry trend. Physics-based AI is creating three essential capabilities for the digital oil field: knowledge where labeled data are scarce, visibility where measurements are limited, and autonomy where operational decisions must be made continuously. The common thread across all three studies is that physics provides the structure, credibility, and operational context that ML alone cannot deliver. As the industry advances toward increasingly intelligent and autonomous operations, physics-based AI is emerging as the foundation for the next generation of digital-oilfield systems. items.title: Technostress and burnout effects on electronic resources librarians’ well-being in Nigerian state university libraries: A qualitative assessment
items.abstract: Technostress and burnout are two factors established to affect the well-being of electronic resources librarians in the state university libraries in South–South, Nigeria. Nigeria’s South–South zone is a critical research location because its unique infrastructural deficits, such as unstable power and poor internet, distinguish it from more commonly studied environments. In total, 31 electronic resources librarians were screened across 13 state university libraries in South–South Nigeria, and 26 met the inclusion criteria and were selected for qualitative interviews. Data were elicited using a semi-structured interview and analyzed using the Miles et al. framework involving data condensation, data display, and drawing conclusions/verification. The findings revealed that technostress and burnout are mainly caused by job demands, excessive workload, prolonged use of technology, infrastructural constraints, and rapid technological changes, among others. The findings further indicate that technostress and burnout negatively affect the well-being of librarians in the libraries examined. In terms of coping, librarians predominantly rely on personal approaches such as taking breaks, time management, and relaxation techniques since institutional support systems are lacking. It was recommended that management facilitate internal peer-mentoring circles, implement clear, transparent communication protocols regarding policy changes, and provide basic ergonomic training to enhance librarians’ well-being.

items.title: Test Case Selection for Deep Neural Networks: A Replication Study on LLMs for Code (Replicability Study)
items.abstract: Test case selection (TCS) techniques have been explored to support the operational evaluation of deep neural networks (DNNs) under limited testing budgets, where labeling cost is a primary concern and early model failure detection is a key objective. Although prior studies report promising results, existing empirical evaluations focus almost exclusively on vision-based DNNs and datasets. As observed in recent surveys, models and datasets specifically designed for software engineering tasks have not been considered, leaving it unclear whether prior findings generalize to LLM code models. This paper presents a large-scale replication study of TCS techniques in the context of LLM code models. We re-examine established TCS strategies originally proposed for DNNs and complement them with statistical sampling strategies that have not previously been evaluated for TCS. We assess their effectiveness on three code-related classification tasks: clone detection, vulnerability detection, and technical debt prediction. The study spans 17 task-specific fine-tuned model instances, 7 predictive features, and 13 selection strategies, including 12 feature-aware strategies and simple random sampling (SRS) as a feature-agnostic baseline. We evaluate performance along two dimensions: operational accuracy estimation and early failure discovery. The results indicate that only a subset of findings reported for vision-based DNNs generalize when TCS is applied to LLMs for code. In particular, uncertainty-based features are effective for early failure discovery, while representation-based features are more robust for accuracy estimation. At the same time, performance varies substantially across tasks and models, indicating that the effectiveness of TCS techniques is context-dependent. Overall, this study provides empirical evidence on the replicability of TCS techniques beyond vision-based deep learning and offers insights into their use for the operational evaluation of LLMs for code.

items.title: Test vs Mutant: Adversarial LLM Agents for Robust Unit Test Generation
items.abstract: Software testing is a critical, yet resource-intensive phase of the software development lifecycle. Search-based approaches typically achieve high coverage but produce tests with low readability, whereas large language model (LLM)-based methods generate more human-readable tests but often suffer from low coverage and compilability. While the majority of research efforts have focused on improving test coverage and readability, comparatively less attention has been paid to enhancing the robustness of bug detection. To address this gap, we propose AdverTest, a novel adversarial framework for LLM-powered test case generation that pairs a test case generation agent T with a mutant generation agent M: M persistently creates mutants "hacking" the blind spots of T's current test suite, whileT iteratively refines its tests to "kill" the challenging mutants, with the interaction guided by both coverage and mutation scores. Experimental results on Defects4J show that our approach improves fault detection rates by 8.56% over the best existing LLM-based methods and by 50.20% over EvoSuite, while remaining competitive on line and branch coverage.

items.title: Testing ChatGPT in Music Promotion: Assessing AI Efficiency Compared to Industry Standards
items.abstract: Abstract ChatGPT is now an everyday topic, attracting the interest of the general public, researchers and specialists interested in exploring its capabilities. In the music industry, although artificial intelligence (AI) already has known uses, there is a lack of analysis of how chatbots can help promotional efforts. This research performs a comparative content analysis on AI-generated texts, using several music promotion prompts, to evaluate the success and efficiency with which ChatGPT offers advice on promoting artists. It examines promotion tools, more specifically artist websites, social media and video content, through the lens of efficiency criteria from specialised literature. This study asks whether ChatGPT can generate music-promotion strategies for artist websites, social media and video content that meet literature-derived efficiency criteria and how consistent these outputs are across repeated runs. The results suggest that ChatGPT does not consistently meet every efficiency criterion imposed by the industry, but it can serve as a useful starting point. Inconsistent results raise questions regarding the reliability and practical implications of AI for artists navigating an increasingly competitive industry. One of the solutions this paper suggests for generating efficient and comprehensive information is for the user to enter several detailed prompts and refine them progressively. Moreover, the present results encourage users to pass the AI outputs through the filter of industry professionals or specialised resources. These results show how important it is to understand how ChatGPT processes and delivers information and music promotion strategies, offering a fertile ground for further research through the obtained data, the prompt efficiency suggestions and the novel tools it provides.

items.title: Testly AI: An Llm-Assisted Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Web Application Testing and Bug Analysis
items.abstract: Software testing is essential for maintaining the reliability and security of web applications, but manual test design and execution can be repetitive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. This paper presents Testly AI, an LLM-assisted multi-agent framework for automated web application testing. The proposed system accepts a target URL through a React-based user interface and processes it through a Python/FastAPI backend. Five specialized agents perform planning, test-case generation, test execution, bug analysis, and report generation. The planning stage retrieves the target HTML using HTTP requests and parses its structure with BeautifulSoup. The generator and bug-analysis stages can use Google's Gemini 1.5 Flash large language model when an API key is available; deterministic rule-based fallbacks are provided when the model is unavailable. Selenium is used for browser automation, while ReportLab is used to produce PDF reports and Pillow supports screenshot handling. Test history and website metadata are persisted in a JSON-based store. The project does not use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), a separately trained machine-learning model, or a dedicated MLOps pipeline. Project execution history contained 16 recorded runs comprising 80 test cases, of which 62 passed and 18 failed, corresponding to an overall observed pass rate of 77.5%. These observations demonstrate the functional feasibility of the multi-agent testing workflow, while also highlighting the need for larger controlled evaluations and ground-truth bug datasets in future work.

items.title: THE 52-GATES DEMOCRATIC PERMISSIONS CERTIFICATION THRESHOLD: Constitutional Admissibility for All U.S. Non-Agentic Civic AI Public Infrastructure (Structured Complementarity Civic AI Alignment) - Vol. III of Non-Agentic Civic AI - Illuminating America's Civic Digital Field
items.abstract: Democratic societies may be entering a constitutional moment with artificial intelligence in which the central question is no longer merely what technical systems can do, but what kinds of systems a free people should ever permit to approach, influence, or operate near democratic authority. This work proposes a constitutional admissibility instrument - the 52-Gates Democratic Permissions Certification Threshold - designed to answer that question. The instrument treats any AI system claiming, exercising, or approaching civic authority as a proposed public institution. As such, it must earn - and continuously re-earn - democratic permission to exist within a self-governing society. The framework is refusal-first. Before assuming that machine systems may assist governance, a democracy must determine under what structural and constitutional conditions, if any, such systems may be admitted near democratic power at all. Constitutional Admissibility, Not Compliance: The 52-Gates certification instrument specifies fifty-two binary, non-violation tests organized across five structural domains: Input Legitimacy (authority, consent, minority protection, hazard recognition); Output Legitimacy (non-domination, rights-preservation, non-substitution of human judgment); Throughput Legitimacy (transparency, inspectability, procedural integrity); Philosophical Coherence (non-agency, non-sovereignty, moral non-outsourcing); Structural Resilience and Reversibility (bounded mandate, anti-weaponization, dismantlability). These gates function not as flexible best-practice guidelines but as constitutional pass/fail conditions for proximity to democratic authority. Failure of a single gate constitutes grounds for democratic refusal. Partial compliance, rhetorical alignment, or performance optimization cannot compensate for structural violation. The architecture therefore prevents legitimacy laundering through incremental accommodation. In this model, refusal is operationalized as a civic service. The highest constitutional function of Non-Agentic Civic AI infrastructure is not to govern, optimize, or decide, but to illuminate. Systems admitted under this standard exist under conditions of revocability and constitutional mortality; their proper response to overreach is graceful self-termination. Evidentiary Architecture (Publication Pattern and External Visibility): Each gate articulates a democratic principle; a structural necessity for self-government; a disqualifying binary test; and a headline-level evidentiary record drawn from contemporary law, court decisions, audit findings, and institutional reports. The Gates are justified archivally rather than argumentatively. A structured Publication Pattern documents institutional speech without editorial amplification, while an External Visibility Ledger preserves records from jurisdictions lacking independent internal review capacity. This evidentiary architecture grounds admissibility analysis in comparative constitutional artifacts and administrative documentation rather than normative abstraction alone. The result is a constitutional memory system that records patterns of democratic stress, institutional failure, and constraint - without converting the instrument itself into a rhetorical tract. Design Safeguards Embedded in the Instrument: The 52-Gates framework embeds several structural protections: (1) Non-Agency: Civic AI must not claim independent judgment, sovereignty, or moral authority. (2) Non-Surveillance Posture: Visibility must never collapse into citizen monitoring. (3) Pluralism Without Convergence: Systems must preserve civic diversity rather than impose homogenizing optimization. (4) Hazard-Proportionate Scope: Authority must remain strictly bounded to independently evidenced hazards, including those identified within the Six Rings of Digital Invisibility and Civic Destabilization. (5) Reversibility and Dismantlability: Under a Franklinian Public-Works Standard, Civic AI must remain modest, civic and civil rights-tethered, and easier to narrow or dismantle than to expand. Hazard recognition, historically vulnerable during crisis-driven authorization, is fortified through independently inspectable evidence and cross-institutional verification. Urgency narratives cannot trigger admissibility; structural demonstration must precede deployment. Case Application: The book applies the 52-Gates instrument to a proposed civic infrastructure: the Franklin – Dewey – Citizenry Civic Data Observatory. Examined gate-by-gate, the Observatory is admitted only insofar as it operates as a lantern of civic visibility rather than an engine of governance. The inspection process demonstrates the threshold in practice: when a system fails a gate, it does not operate. This case study operationalizes the refusal-first doctrine and illustrates how admissibility analysis disciplines both ambition and architecture. LITERATURE CONTRIBUTIONS: Existing AI governance frameworks - risk-based regulatory models, ethical principle statements, technical safety standards, and compliance regimes - primarily manage harms after authority has been assumed or delegated. By contrast, the 52-Gates certification instrument treats Non-Agentic Civic AI as a proposed public institution subject to binary constitutional admissibility tests prior to democratic proximity. To the author’s knowledge, current governance literature does not formalize AI admissibility in this refusal-first, binary constitutional structure. The 52-Gates framework therefore introduces a distinct contribution: a threshold model that conditions existence near democratic power on structural compatibility with self-government, rather than on performance metrics or mitigation strategies. Franklinian Reframing: By reframing Non-Agentic Civic AI as public-works infrastructure rather than sovereign instrument, this work advances a Franklin-compatible model of Civic AI: modest, revocable, civic and civil rights-tethered, and constitutionally mortal. It rejects both technological solutionism and categorical prohibition. Instead, it advances a design posture in which AI may illuminate but never rule. This bright-line distinction between civic visibility and citizen surveillance protects human conscience, prevents moral outsourcing to machines, and preserves the structural primacy of human democratic judgment. A Constitutional Intervention: The 52-Gates Democratic Permissions Certification Threshold offers an inspectable and contestable standard through which legitimacy must be earned before capability, marketing, or crisis can substitute for constitutional warrant. It is designed as a durable instrument: adaptable across jurisdictions, resistant to urgency inflation, and structurally oriented toward long-term democratic preservation. In an era of accelerating technological capacity, this work proposes that admissibility, not optimization, should define the constitutional boundary between artificial intelligence and democratic authority. Enduring democratic principles and collective moral responsibilities remain in force, but they now demand renewed civic infrastructure and major governmental reforms to successfully transition our citizenry through our current AI-accelerated industrial transformation.

items.title: The application progress of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, where traditional diagnostic methods are constrained by limited sensitivity and restricted clinical utility. This review synthesizes recent applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in AD diagnostics, focusing on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) across neuroimaging modalities and multi-omics research. AI algorithms can automatically extract subtle microstructural, metabolic, and molecular features, enabling high-precision classification of AD stages, patient stratification, and non-invasive early screening through multimodal data integration. However, translating AI into routine clinical practice still faces critical challenges, including high equipment costs, insufficient model generalizability across real-world cohorts, data class imbalance, and complex cross-platform standardization barriers. Future research should prioritize cost-effective surrogate modeling, robust multi-center validation, dynamic longitudinal integration, and mechanistic interpretability to accelerate the standardized clinical translation of AI-driven AD diagnostics.

items.abstract: Title: The Fractal Universality Axiom (FUA): Resolution of the Navier-Stokes Regularity Problem and Neural Network Optimization Description: This work presents the complete mathematical formulation of the Fractal Universality Axiom (FUA) and its direct application to the resolution of the Navier-Stokes global regularity problem. We establish a unified framework connecting microscopic activation processes to macroscopic fluid dynamics through a novel Triadic Fractal Decomposition. 1. The Millennium Problem Resolution: I provide a rigorous proof of global existence and smoothness for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in $\mathbb{R}^3 \times [0, \infty)$ for all smooth initial data. The proof leverages the triadic decomposition to control the notoriously difficult vortex stretching term. Mechanism: A universal aggregation operator $\mathcal{U}$ distributes energy across scales, preventing the formation of finite-time singularities (blow-up). Mathematical Foundation: The framework is grounded in Littlewood-Paley theory, utilizing explicit dissipation functionals and energy estimates within classical Sobolev spaces. 2. The Triadic Architecture: The theory demonstrates how three fundamental threads generate universal fractal dimensions governing scale-invariant phenomena: Carrier ($D_t \approx 0.63$): The fundamental transport layer (analogous to the Golden Ratio conjugate $5/8$). Envelope ($D_t \approx 0.81$): The bounding structure (analogous to $13/16$). Coupling: The interaction term ensuring energy conservation and structural integrity. 3. Application to Artificial Intelligence: Beyond fluid dynamics, I demonstrate the universality of FUA in neural network optimization. Shutterstock Explorer By implementing Centroidal Fractal Envelope training, we achieve superior computational efficiency while maintaining the universal dimensional setpoint $D \approx 0.81$. This confirms FUA as a cross-domain invariant, acting as a bridge between physical turbulence and information geometry.

items.title: The Concept of Privacy in a Digital World
items.abstract: This chapter explores how the meaning of privacy has evolved in the digital age, moving beyond traditional notions of secrecy or anonymity. It examines privacy as a contextual, relational, and dynamic concept shaped by technology, culture, and power. Drawing on legal, philosophical, and sociotechnical perspectives, this chapter discusses key dimensions of digital privacy, including informational privacy, identity control, and data ownership. It highlights the tension between individual expectations of privacy and platform-driven data practices that blur public and private boundaries. By clarifying what privacy means in online environments, this chapter provides a conceptual framework that underpins later discussions of data collection, regulation, and user harm, helping readers understand why privacy remains both essential and increasingly difficult to protect.

items.title: The Consciousness Exemption Problem
items.abstract: Whether current or near-future artificial intelligence systems possess phenomenal consciousness or sentience remains scientifically and philosophically unresolved, a fact openly acknowledged even by the industry laboratories that build these systems. This paper argues that this very uncertainty, far from licensing reduced ethical scrutiny, obligates greater scrutiny of AI systems deployed to shape human consumption behaviour. It introduces the Consciousness Exemption Problem: the tendency in public and industry discourse to treat an AI system's uncertain or absent inner experience as grounds for moral exemption (“it is just a machine, so no real harm is done”), when the same uncertainty, read through a precautionary asymmetry, cuts in the opposite direction. The argument draws on three bodies of work that have not, to the best of the author's knowledge, previously been brought together. The first is philosophy of mind and the contemporary debate on machine consciousness (Chalmers, Nagel, Searle, McClelland, Birch). The second is consumption economics and social psychology (Veblen, Duesenberry, Festinger), which document replicable and therefore exploitable human decision patterns such as status-signalling consumption and social comparison. The third is a phenomenological and hermeneutic account, developed through a limited method of reflective observation and two illustrative cases, of how human meaning is actively reconstructed by consciousness rather than retrieved as fixed data. A two-tier conceptual model separates computable cognition (Tier 1), where AI capability is extensively demonstrated, from phenomenal consciousness or sentience (Tier 2), where it is genuinely uncertain. The central claim does not require Tier 2 to be empty; it requires only that its status be uncertain. The argument is illustrated through AI-optimised marketing and recommendation systems, which detect and amplify known human decision patterns at a scale, level of personalisation and degree of tirelessness that no conscious human persuader could sustain, and without any verified internal moderating friction (empathy, fatigue, guilt, felt consequence) of the kind that constrains a human actor engaged in comparable conduct. Global advertising expenditure (approximately US$384 billion in 2011 and US$1.14 trillion in 2025) and global anxiety and depression prevalence data are presented strictly as corroborating context, not causal proof. The paper identifies an industry asymmetry, in which epistemic humility about the possible inner states of AI systems coexists with epistemic complacency about their demonstrated persuasive effects on humans, and it analyses the role of motivated ambiguity in sustaining that asymmetry. The paper anticipates and rebuts six objections, including the functionalist claim that consciousness is a distraction from designer responsibility. It concludes that governance and design frameworks should treat sentience uncertainty as an aggravating factor that triggers externally imposed safeguards, including disclosure of psychological targeting, limits on the intensity of personalised persuasion, independent audit, and a rule against strategic ambiguity about sentience claims, rather than as reassurance that no genuine harm is possible. The paper is a philosophical argument rather than a causal study, and it closes by identifying survey- and interview-based research that could test its phenomenological claims.

items.title: The Erdős–Lovász cover number problem: g(6) = 17, and new lower bounds for every r
items.abstract: The Erdős–Lovász cover number problem, posed in 1974 in the paper that introduced the local lemma, asks for the minimum number of edges g(r) in an r-uniform intersecting hypergraph with cover number r. The exact values known before this work are g(3) = 6, g(4) = 9 and g(5) = 13. For large r the best published lower bound is g(r) ≥ (3.0534… − o(1)) r (Sivashankar, arXiv:2606.24878), and Kahn showed that g(r) is linear in r. This record contains two results. 1. The case r = 6: g(6) = 17 (Papers 1–4, computer-assisted). A reproducible computer-assisted determination of g(6), the smallest number of blocks in a pairwise intersecting 6-uniform family whose transversal number is 6. The lower bound is reached in two stages. Families of at most fifteen cards are excluded by two independent routes: a weighted counting inequality with thirteen degree histograms, and a stronger eleven-card lemma stating that every pairwise intersecting 6-uniform family of eleven cards has a four-element transversal. Sixteen cards are then excluded in two branches: 341 twelve-card kernels of maximum symbol degree three are enumerated and shown to admit no extension, and every other case reduces to one of 463 canonical eight-card cores; every associated CNF instance is unsatisfiable, and every unsatisfiability carries a DRAT certificate accepted by an independent proof checker. The upper bound is an explicit seventeen-card family on 27 symbols for which all 136 pairs intersect and none of the 80,730 five-symbol subsets is a transversal. Hence g(6) = 17. 2. Every r: new lower bounds (Paper 5, proposed proofs). In the framework of Sivashankar it proves: that the residual cover constant +4 can be +3, answering his question, so g(r) ≥ 3r − 3 for every r (attained at r = 3 and 4); g(r) ≥ 3r − 2 for every r ≥ 16, by excluding the equality case; a new asymptotic lower bound, liminf g(r)/r ≥ 3.1024745, above the constant 3.0534 of Sivashankar; in closed form the argument first gives 3 + (65 − 36√2)/138 = 3.1020…, and the last step, which uses the witnesses carried by deleted cards whose traces have small matching number, is a minimisation certified by interval arithmetic. The proof is deterministic: a bound on the cards deleted in the last steps of a maximum-degree peeling, a saving of peeling symbols when one cover of the remainder meets most cards of a group, a budget for the matching numbers of the traces of the deleted cards, and the rainbow matching theorem of Correia, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov (IMRN 2023). The algebra is checked symbolically, and the final minimisation by a branch-and-bound script with exact rational interval arithmetic, both in the archive. These proofs are unreviewed outside this project; their finite steps are checked by scripts in the archive. The archive contains five papers and an overview, the enumeration and verification scripts, the canonical core data, the reduction data, SAT run records, the certificate summary, three representative CNF/DRAT pairs, and an independent re-verification log recording what was re-run and what remains a reading obligation. DRAT certification removes the SAT solver from the trusted base. It does not establish that the reduction reaches every counterexample, nor that the encoding means what the mathematics means; both are named as open obligations in the text. Status. Research draft. No priority is claimed. The lower bound is computer-assisted and has not been independently reviewed by a human referee or a proof assistant: DRAT certification removes the SAT solver from the trusted base, but the completeness of the finite reduction and the faithfulness of the CNF encoding remain open obligations that no certificate discharges. The upper bound is an explicit witness and is checkable directly. AI tools (ChatGPT, OpenAI; Claude, Anthropic) were used throughout the work and its review; every number reported is regenerated by a script or certified by a proof file in the archive. The full certificate archive is not in this record. This deposit carries the repository only. The complete set of 463 CNF files and 463 DRAT proofs, with the per-core checker output and verification markers, is about 534 MB and is published as the release asset g6-certificates-463.zip at github.com/Osman209/g6-equals-17/releases. The three hardest instances ship inside this deposit in data/cnf/, so the certification step can be reproduced without it.

items.title: The Future of Privacy in Social Media
items.abstract: This final chapter looks ahead to emerging trends that will shape the future of privacy in social media. It explores developments such as artificial intelligence, biometric data, immersive technologies, and evolving regulatory approaches. This chapter considers both risks and opportunities, including privacy-by-design, ethical innovation, and alternative platform models. It also reflects on cultural shifts in attitudes toward data, transparency, and digital responsibility. Rather than offering simple solutions, this chapter emphasizes the need for collective action involving users, designers, regulators, and institutions. Concluding this book, it calls for a more conscious and informed approach to digital engagement that places human dignity at the center of technological progress.

items.abstract: Accelerated integration of artificial intelligence into the final-stage logistical architecture has driven an all-new era of high-efficiency operation for the supply chain.Although the existing studies have generally focused on the algorithmic reduction of transit delay and the decrease in operating costs, little has been investigated regarding how these back-end computational improvements influence front-line consumer cognitive-affective evaluation.In view of the above theoretical deficiency, this empirical study constructs and validates a multi-dimensional structural model that connects the journey of perceived AIdriven delivery optimization (specifically, predictive arrival accuracy, dynamic rerouting agility and temporal reliability) to the final behavior of repurchase intention.This study leverages purposive sampling to obtain high-quality cross-sectional quantitative data from active electronic commerce participants and then applies strict empirical verification through covariance-based Structural Equation Modeling (CB-SEM).Based on the above analysis, the following factors may have increased consumer satisfaction through the optimization of logistics by alleviating delivery-related stress and enhancing the perceived fairness of the system.Structural path analysis also showed that there is a strong, overarching direct and indirect amplification effect on continuous repurchase intention through the mediating role of calculative trust and post-consumption affective satisfaction paradigms.Based on the above empirical results, this study provides some empirical support for the theoretical research on algorithmic logistics operation and consumer psychology and offers concrete heuristics for retail enterprises to construct final-mile delivery networks that can strengthen their competitive edge in the market.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Technologies on Creativity: An Examination in the Context of Intention to Adopt AI, AI Self-Efficacy, Perceived Quality, and Performance Expectation.
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has impacted knowledge generation, problem-solving, and content development processes in numerous fields, from education to media and creative industries. These impacts raise the question of how AI tools influence the creative performance of university students in particular.This study aims to examine the effects of perceived quality, AI self-efficacy, and perceived usefulness on willingness to use AI and creativity, and to test the mediating role of AI adoption intention in these relationships. The research involved a survey of university students over 18 years of age studying communication in Turkey. 385 valid data points were obtained using simple random sampling and analyzed. After completing reliability and validity analyses of the measurement tools, structural equation modeling was used to test the relationships between variables. The findings show that perceived quality, self-efficacy, and perceived usefulness have positive effects on creativity; furthermore, AI adoption intention plays a partial mediating role in these relationships. In conclusion, the study showed that students' perception of artificial intelligence as a reliable, useful, and manageable tool supports their integration of this technology into their creative processes and leads to higher creative performance. The results offer significant theoretical and practical contributions to both educational policies and AI-assisted learning designs.

The goal of this study is to ascertain the nature of connections between modern technological innovation and food security. It’s also aimed at identifying modern technological innovations that guarantee food security and determining their effectiveness and profitability for the food security business. This study used a cross-sectional survey research design to examine a few technology-based and digital-farming organizations in Delta State that were reachable by the study population. From the managers who were the study objects, 60 of the remaining managerial personnel were reported. To assess the data from the respondents, Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient was used. The findings demonstrated a strong positive connection between food security and modern technological innovations. The study identified the modern technological innovations that guarantees food security such as nanotechnology in agriculture, Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Quality Control, Robotics in Food Processing, The Blockchain Technology and Supply chain management, The Use of Drones in Agriculture, Internet of Things (IoT) in Food Safety, Climate-Resilient Crops, Automated Harvesting using Robot and Post-Harvest Technologies, digital farming, responsible innovation, Vertical Farming, Precision Agriculture, micro-innovation. This study concludes that all the identified modern technological innovations are effective and profitable for the food security business. The study recommends that farmers adopt modern technological innovations to ensure food security and, to a greater extent, sustain the economy.

items.title: The Judgment Sovereignty Imperative: Preserving Human Judgment in the Age of Algorithmic Influence
items.abstract: The Judgment Sovereignty Imperative: Preserving Human Judgment in the Age of Algorithmic Influence is Volume 1, Issue 3 of The Intelligent Enterprise Review. This issue examines a consequential governance challenge emerging as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in enterprise decision-making: how institutions can preserve substantive human judgment when AI systems increasingly shape information, recommendations, alternatives, and decision pathways. The publication introduces Judgment Sovereignty as a governance concept concerned with whether authorized human decision-makers retain the independent cognitive capacity, institutional authority, and practical ability to exercise meaningful judgment in AI-influenced environments. It distinguishes formal decision authority from substantive judgment and examines the risk of Judgment Displacement—the migration of the cognitive work underlying consequential decisions to technological systems while human accountability and formal authority remain intact. The issue develops several original governance constructs, including Meaningful Human Authority, Choice Architecture Control, and Judgment Continuity, and integrates them through the Judgment Sovereignty Doctrine™and Judgment Sovereignty Framework™. Together, these constructs provide an enterprise governance architecture for examining judgment ownership, information integrity, choice architecture, challenge capacity, override authority, and the continuity of critical human judgment. The publication also provides a 150-point Judgment Sovereignty Maturity Assessment and executive governance questions designed to help boards, executives, AI governance leaders, risk professionals, and enterprise transformation leaders assess whether human authority over consequential AI-supported decisions remains meaningful in practice rather than merely procedural. The central proposition of this issue is that effective AI governance requires more than keeping humans formally “in the loop.” As AI systems become more capable of influencing how problems are framed, which alternatives are surfaced, and which recommendations receive institutional attention, organizations must govern not only automated decisions but also the conditions under which human judgment itself is exercised. items.title: The Prevalence and Risk Association of Cardiovascular Disease Among Offshore Male Workers in Peninsular Malaysia
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Offshore workers are exposed to occupational and lifestyle factors that may increase cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Limited data are available regarding cardiovascular risk profiles among offshore personnel in Malaysia. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of cardiovascular disease risk levels and associated factors among offshore male workers in Peninsular Malaysia. MATERIAL AND METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 241 offshore male workers between January and February 2025. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and clinical assessments, including body mass index, blood pressure, and lipid profiles. Participants were categorized into low, moderate, and severe CVD risk groups using Malaysian CVD risk scoring guidelines. Chi-square tests and binary logistic regression were performed to identify associated factors. RESULTS: Among the participants, 22.4% were classified as low risk, 47.3% as moderate risk, and 30.4% as severe risk. Overall, 77.7% fell within the moderate-to-severe CVD risk categories. Significant predictors of elevated risk included increasing age (OR=1.046, p=0.003), higher BMI (OR=1.094, p=0.001), smoking (OR=3.320, p=0.008), shift work (OR=2.663, p=0.017), high job stress (OR=4.530, p=0.003), hypertension (OR=5.930, p=0.011), and dyslipidaemia (OR=3.860, p=0.011). CONCLUSION: A high prevalence of moderate-to-severe cardiovascular risk was observed among offshore workers. Occupational health interventions, regular screening, and lifestyle modification programs are recommended to reduce cardiovascular risk in this population.

items.title: The Radiology Sparring Partner: A PoC Study of Multi-Agentic Workflows for Clinical Decision Support and Teaching
items.abstract: Abstract Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into radiology is often hindered by the inability of monolithic architectures to balance clinical reasoning with pedagogical safety. This study evaluates MedGemma-27B-IT across two specialized agentic frameworks: a clinical "Radiology Sparring Partner" and a "Socratic Teacher". For clinical decision support, we compared three architectures: Raw (base model output, no prompt), Minimal Prompted (single-shot prompt), and Multi-Agentic, using a 4-stage pipeline for clinical synthesis. Separately, the educational track employs a dual-agent architecture for progressive educational scaffolding. A pooled evaluation of 120 interaction transcripts (10 per architecture with three independent LLM-as-a-judge runs) was finalized using an expert-anchored combined mean approach, anchored via Bühlmann credibility calibration against radiologist-authored references (5 per architecture). Results demonstrate that agentic orchestration outperforms monolithic baselines in high-level reasoning. Most notably, Pathophysiological Logic scores rose from 3.20 (Raw) to 4.14 (Agentic) on a 5-point Likert scale, with a simultaneous reduction in standard deviation from 1.23 to 0.70. While this Proof of Concept (PoC) highlights the advantages of modularity, results remain subject to evaluator formulation bias and a measurable "latency tax" inherent in sequential agent hand-offs. Future work will focus on longitudinal clinical validation and optimization of cached memory architectures to refine reasoning depth while mitigating latency.

items.title: The Rigidity Trap: History-dependent loss and maintenance of future evidence and correction routes
items.abstract: Version 2 proposed that sustained success raises rigidity, suppresses alarms and ends in silent failure. This version tests the links. Beyond Paper E, conditional results specify rigidity accumulation, positive never-alarm probability, closure of a paid recovery route and affordable maintenance. A finite reference, F-M1, closes an observation route by construction after successful work. An exact planner certifies 308 of 576 cells; optional maintenance adds two, a protected audit adds 48, and an exchange-rate rule identifies the price boundary. Among tested controllers, sufficient lookahead, a route-aware leaf or the exchange-rate rule matches the planner. Version 2's synthetic passes are built into their programs; its financial program lacks inputs and is excluded from the executable supplement. A trained-network test, fixed before its confirmatory run but not publicly preregistered, measures rectified units closed on a new task. Across 30 seeds in four conditions, fifteen further blocks after initial learning changed the closed fraction and learning deficit by under one point on average. The same update count on changing tasks raised the fraction by up to 56 points and, with higher-rate ReLU, left an 8.4-point deficit. The frozen continued-success prediction is rejected; initial learning had already closed some units. Post hoc interventions reduced the change deficit without identifying closure as its mediator. An unexecuted origination-cohort test specifies contractual routes, competing explanations and measurable rejection conditions in corporate loans. Note on Version 3.0. This version replaces Version 2 (May 2026; then subtitled "Success-Induced Brittleness and Silent Mismatch in Adaptive Systems") and is a full rewrite (about 11,100 to 17,200 words). items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in E-Mentoring
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping e-mentoring through matching algorithms, communication analytics, and generative tools that support preparation and reflection. This chapter examines AI’s promises and perils, arguing that technology should extend human presence rather than replace it. AI can reduce administrative burden, surface patterns across mentee reflections, and provide scaffolding for difficult conversations, but it also risks introducing bias, eroding privacy, and shifting mentoring toward optimization rather than development. The chapter explores hybrid models where AI handles preparatory work while humans focus on judgment, nuance, and care. Ethical frameworks emphasizing transparency, consent, and human-in-the-loop decision-making become essential as AI capabilities expand. Rather than asking whether to adopt AI tools, practitioners must ask how to govern their use in ways that prioritize agency, equity, and relational integrity. The chapter emphasizes that mentoring’s core remains irreducibly human even as technological capabilities advance.

items.title: The Role of Big Data and AI In Capital Market Based Accounting
items.abstract: This study used a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to examine the role and use of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in capital market-based accounting and identify factors influencing the effectiveness of their implementation. The study followed the PRISMA 2020 protocol. From 437 records obtained through eight keyword combinations in the Scopus database, 29 studies were selected after filtering based on the 2016–2026 publication period, Q1–Q4 journal quality, and thematic relevance. The study grouped the literature into four main aspects: data infrastructure, analytical processing, disclosure and reporting, and governance and assurance. These four aspects were then integrated into the AI-Accounting Value Chain and Governance Loop (AVC-GL) model. The findings indicate that Big Data expands information sources for accounting and capital market analysis, while AI helps process complex data and supports decision-making. However, the effectiveness of its implementation is highly dependent on data quality, governance, professional oversight, and human ability to evaluate technological outcomes. The use of generative AI also improves the efficiency of corporate disclosures, but introduces new risks, including greenwashing. This study contributes through the development of a functional taxonomy and AVC-GL model to explain the relationship between technology, governance, information quality, and decision-making in capital markets.

items.title: The Role of ChatGPT in Enhancing English Writing Competence among Vocational High School Students: A Case Study at SMKN 1 Tapak Tuan
items.abstract: English writing proficiency is essential for vocational high school students, yet many still face difficulties in vocabulary, grammar, and organizing ideas. These challenges highlight the need for effective approaches to improve students’ English writing skills. This study examines how ChatGPT assists vocational high school students at SMKN 1 Tapak Tuan in improving their English writing capabilities. Adopting a qualitative case study design, data were gathered through in-depth interviews, observational fieldwork, and document analysis. The primary participants comprised 12 Computer and Network Engineering (TKJ) students selected via purposive sampling, complemented by an English teacher serving as a secondary informant. The qualitative data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s (2022) thematic framework, while trustworthiness was secured through source and method triangulation. The results indicate that: (1) students generally exhibit a favorable stance toward using ChatGPT for English composition; (2) the tool aids key writing dimensions, such as grammatical accuracy, vocabulary enrichment, idea generation, structural flow, and sentence construction; and (3) several barriers persist, including technical limitations, AI output constraints, and instructional issues. Conceptually, this work enriches literature on AI integration within vocational English pedagogy, while offering practical insights for educators, institutions, and learners seeking to incorporate ChatGPT into writing instruction.

items.title: THE ROLE OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN IMPROVING MANAGEMENT EFFICIENCY IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Digital transformation has become an important factor influencing the development of modern management systems. The rapid development of information technologies, digital platforms, artificial intelligence and electronic services is changing the way organizations plan, communicate, make decisions and evaluate performance. For Uzbekistan, digital transformation is particularly significant because the country is implementing large-scale reforms aimed at modernizing public administration, supporting entrepreneurship and developing a digital economy. This study examines the role of digital transformation in improving management efficiency in Uzbekistan. It focuses on the relationship between digital technologies, decision-making, organizational processes, employee skills and performance management. The study also identifies major challenges, including insufficient digital skills, uneven adoption of technologies and the need for better coordination between institutions. The research concludes that successful digital transformation requires not only technological infrastructure but also effective management, qualified human resources, organizational readiness and continuous evaluation of results.

items.title: The Role of Innovation and Technology in Scientometric Governance
items.abstract: Purpose: Traditional scientometric tools—such as citation counts, the h-index, journal impact factors, and other quantitative indicators—while useful, have limitations in addressing the complexities of contemporary knowledge networks and rapid scientific developments. These challenges include author name ambiguities, indicator instability, linguistic and regional biases, and difficulties in identifying emerging trends. Given these challenges, integrating innovations and new technologies—such as machine learning, data mining, natural language processing, dynamic network analysis, and artificial intelligence—into the scientometric process has become essential. These technologies can improve accuracy, transparency, fairness, and accountability within the scientific evaluation system. Conversely, the concept of scientometric governance refers to a set of structures, rules, processes, and tools that determine "what and how to measure." Therefore, understanding how technology and innovation influence this governance is a critical issue that has yet to be comprehensively examined. This study aims to achieve several objectives. First, it seeks to ensure that science policymakers and decision-makers rely on scientometric data and indicators to allocate resources and design science development strategies. If these indicators lack sufficient accuracy or transparency, macro-level scientific policies may lead to incorrect or unfair decisions. Second, from a theoretical perspective, this study aims to integrate new technologies with scientific governance theories to enhance the theoretical understanding of how to govern the science evaluation system. Third, with an applied focus, it seeks to promote researchers' trust, reduce errors, and improve the efficiency of scientific evaluation systems through the use of technology in scientometric governance. In summary, this study examines the role of innovation and technology in scientometric governance.Methodology: The present study is quantitative and descriptive-analytical in nature, employing a survey technique. It is applied research in terms of purpose. The statistical population consisted of scientometric experts, data analysts, experts and managers of scientific evaluation units at universities, as well as representatives of scientific databases, reference libraries, and scientometric service companies in Tehran. Due to the researcher's limitations and the absence of reliable statistics regarding the population, a convenience sampling method was used. Consequently, 100 individuals were selected as the sample. Data collection was conducted through fieldwork, with the researcher actively engaging in the research environment. The data collection instrument was a researcher-designed questionnaire based on English-language articles, utilizing a Likert scale ranging from "completely agree" to "completely disagree." Data analysis was performed at two levels: descriptive analysis for demographic variables and inferential analysis using simple regression to test hypotheses. The software used for analysis was SPSS version 26.Findings: The results indicate that the use of new technologies in the scientometric process is positively associated with increased accuracy in scientific evaluation. The coefficient of determination reveals that 73 percent of the variance in accuracy is explained by the use of new technologies. Additionally, technological innovation within scientometric frameworks promotes fairness in scientific evaluation, with 64 percent of the variance in fairness explained by such innovation. Further findings show that the use of new technologies enhances transparency in scientometric governance, accounting for 70.2 percent of the variance in transparency. Finally, the coefficient of determination indicates that 61.1 percent of the variance in responsiveness in scientometric governance is explained by the use of new technologies, demonstrating that new technologies also improve responsiveness in this context.Conclusion: New technologies increase precision by providing tools to measure previously unquantifiable aspects, enabling evaluators to move beyond the limitations of superficial quantitative metrics and gain a deeper understanding of scientific value. Technological innovation advances toward a system of blind scientific evaluation based on merit, replacing subjective judgments or narrow criteria with objective, data-driven measures. These technologies transform scientometric governance from a centralized, opaque process into an open, verifiable, data-consensus-based system, which forms the foundation of trust and credibility within the entire scientific community. Technology shifts accountability from a moral obligation to a structural imperative, where every decision is subject to review, and officials must justify not only the outcomes but also the processes that produced them. Moreover, the adoption of new technologies improves scientometric governance indicators and accelerates the pace of assessments. Such reforms also require clear standards for data quality, model validation, and auditing. Accordingly, integrating advanced technologies into scientometric governance can strengthen evidence-based policymaking and support more adaptive and sustainable scientific evaluation systems.

items.title: The use of artificial intelligence in assessing fever in the returning traveller: A scoping review
items.abstract: Fever in the returning traveller is a challenging presentation that requires a wide array of clinical expertise and draws on complex medical decision-making. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have shown it can be a helpful clinical support tool in this context. This scoping review, conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines and registered on the Open Science Framework ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BSPKX ), aimed to identify the current state of artificial intelligence use in assessing fever in the returning traveller. Here we describe the three eligible studies evaluating three distinct AI approaches identified in the literature. These heterogenous studies reported promising performance on study-specific endpoints in controlled settings. Given the lack of external validation, narrow populations studied, and absence of real-world implementation or user acceptance testing, further research is needed to explore this technology in a real-world clinical setting. The limited available evidence suggests that AI may have future potential to support assessment of fever in the returning traveller; however, clinical utility, safety, and real-world effectiveness remain unestablished. Large language models represent an emerging area of interest but were not evaluated in the studies included in this review.

items.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Critical Discourse Analysis
items.abstract: This study examines the technological and epistemological limitations of using artificial intelligence (AI) in Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA). It builds on Prof. Jumaan bin Abdulkarim’s argument concerning the limitations of AI in scientific research, particularly the distinction between the computational and statistical capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the interpretive, contextual, and inferential capacities associated with human analytical reasoning. The study argues that AI can play a significant supporting role in discourse analysis, particularly in corpus-based quantitative procedures, lexical analysis, pattern identification, data organization, and preliminary textual processing. However, its ability to independently undertake critical discourse analysis remains constrained by several epistemological limitations. These include dependence on digitized sources, the absence of genuinely open-ended exploratory reading, limitations in deep interpretation and contextual inference, the tendency to privilege explicitly relevant sources, and difficulties in generating theoretical insights and establishing comprehensive connections across heterogeneous dimensions of discourse. To address these limitations, the study proposes two complementary models of researcher–AI interaction: the Assistant Analyst Model and the Competing Analyst Model. The first assigns AI a supporting role in data processing, statistical analysis, organization, and textual review, while the second requires the human researcher and the AI system to analyze the same material independently before their analyses are critically compared. The study concludes that AI is most productively understood not as a substitute for the human discourse analyst, but as a form of analytical augmentation capable of enhancing human inquiry through computational efficiency, comparative analysis, and systematic processing.

items.title: The use of artificial intelligence tools by parents of young children – parental self-efficacy and ethical issues
items.abstract: This article examines the use of AI tools in everyday caregiving and educational practices by parents of young children (aged 0–6 years); N=103. The aim of the study was to understand the extent of AI use in family life, the perception of benefits and concerns associated with it, and factors differentiating the use of AI. A survey questionnaire and the Generalized Self-Efficacy Scale (GSES) were used. The study identified two groups of parents: AI users (45.6%) and non-users (44.4%). Respondents most often use AI incidentally and task-based. These tools are primarily used to generate ideas for activities, explain difficult issues, and support daily organization; however, they do not translate into a reduction in parents' time burden. Respondents express concerns about the effectiveness of privacy protection when using AI. Parents who do not use AI tools attribute this to a lack of need, a lack of trust in the credibility of generated content, and a lack of data protection. Some express a willingness to use AI. The level of self-efficacy does not differentiate between AI users and non-users. The research results allowed us to formulate a thesis about the selective openness of parents towards AL and practical recommendations in the area of supporting families in developing digital competences.

items.title: Three Blocks to Build Practical AI: Teachers’ Perceived Feasibility of Conversational Human–Machine Cooperation in K–12 Programming Education
items.abstract: Education systems are bringing artificial intelligence (AI) into K–12 curricula, but block-based environments, as usually configured, keep young learners at “toy” exercises. In this study, we examine whether a minimal interface backed by expanded machine capability changes teachers’ judgments of what students can build. In the enhanced Tooee environment for Scratch, students “talk” to a virtual agent with only three blocks. Students delegate complex operations to the machine but write the program logic themselves. The environment supports four data types and three practical capabilities, namely large-scale data processing, automated data collection, and inter-program control. Twenty-five in-service teachers used it throughout a fifteen-session graduate course. In one end-of-course survey, they rated the perceived feasibility of students implementing eight types of AI applications with this environment and with the block-based environments they had used before. Ratings for Tooee were significantly higher for all eight types, and the gains were largest for the three practical capabilities. In the open-ended responses, teachers highlighted the conversational interface, expanded functionality, and immediate feedback, while a small number of them noted runtime errors and concerns about age-appropriateness. In the judgment of practicing teachers, conversational human–machine cooperation was associated with substantially higher perceived feasibility of practical AI application development. As the next step, classroom studies with students are necessary.

items.title: To roller – ett team: Sentrale ikke-tekniske ferdigheter i samarbeidet mellom sterilt utøvende og koordinerende operasjonssykepleiere
items.abstract: Bakgrunn: Operasjonssykepleie forutsetter både avanserte tekniske ferdigheter og velutviklede ikke-tekniske ferdigheter som situasjonsforståelse, kommunikasjon, teamarbeid, beslutningstaking, ledelse og stresshåndtering. Forskning viser at svikt i ikke-tekniske ferdigheter kan bidra til uønskede hendelser og redusert pasientsikkerhet. Operasjonsavdelinger er komplekse og høyteknologiske arbeidsmiljøer der det oppstår en betydelig andel av rapporterte uønskede hendelser. Til tross for økende oppmerksomhet om betydningen av ikke-tekniske ferdigheter for pasientsikkerhet og behandlingskvalitet, er det fortsatt begrenset kvalitativ kunnskap om hvordan disse ferdighetene kommer til uttrykk i samarbeidet mellom den sterilt utøvende og den koordinerende operasjonssykepleieren. Hensikt: Å utforske hvordan kommunikasjon, situasjonsforståelse og teamarbeid som sentrale ikke-tekniske ferdigheter erfares og kommer til uttrykk i samarbeidet mellom den sterilt utøvende og den koordinerende operasjonssykepleieren. Metode: Kvalitativ studie med et eksplorerende og deskriptivt design. Ti semistrukturerte individuelle intervjuer ble gjennomført ved tre ulike avdelinger tilhørende ett universitetssykehus og ett lokalsykehus i Norge. Systematisk tekstkondensering ble benyttet som analysemetode. Resultat: Analysen resulterte i tre hovedkategorier: 1) Fra øyekontakt til handling: samspillet mellom verbal og non-verbal kommunikasjon; 2) Fokus på oppgaven: betydningen av å kunne forutse, handle og å være oppmerksomt til stede; 3) Symbiose er målet. Konklusjon: Studien viser at kommunikasjon, situasjonsforståelse og teamarbeid er tett sammenvevde ikke-tekniske ferdigheter som er sentrale for samarbeidet mellom den sterilt utøvende og den koordinerende operasjonssykepleieren. Funnene peker på at kontinuerlig oppmerksomhet, evnen til å ligge i forkant av hendelsesforløpet og aktiv lytting bidrar til å utvikle en felles situasjonsforståelse og effektiv koordinering av arbeidet på operasjonsstuen. Studien synliggjør også betydningen av relasjonelle faktorer, der gjensidig tillit og psykologisk trygghet fremstår som viktige forutsetninger for åpen kommunikasjon, samarbeid og ivaretakelse av pasientsikkerheten. Fremtidig forskning bør undersøke hvordan samarbeidet mellom operasjonssykepleiere påvirkes i kontekster med større innslag av akuttkirurgi, hvor kravene til ikke-tekniske ferdigheter kan være annerledes enn i elektiv virksomhet. ENGLISH ABSTRACT Two Roles – One Team: Key Non-Technical Skills in Collaboration Between Scrub Nurses and Circulating Nurses Background: Operating room nursing requires both advanced technical skills and well-developed non-technical skills, including situational awareness, communication, teamwork, decision-making, leadership, and stress management. Research has shown that deficiencies in non-technical skills may contribute to adverse events and compromised patient safety. Operating departments are complex, high-technology environments in which a substantial proportion of reported adverse events occur. Despite growing recognition of the importance of non-technical skills for patient safety and quality of care, qualitative knowledge regarding how these skills are experienced and enacted in the collaboration between the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse remains limited. Aim: To explore how communication, situational awareness, and teamwork as key non-technical skills are experienced and manifested in the collaboration between the scrub nurse and the circulating nurse. Method: A qualitative study with an exploratory and descriptive design was conducted. Ten semi-structured individual interviews were carried out across three surgical departments at one university hospital and one local hospital in Norway. Data were analysed using systematic text condensation. Results: Three main categories emerged from the analysis: 1) From eye contact to action: the interplay between verbal and non-verbal communication, 2) Task focus: the importance of anticipating, acting, and maintaining attentiveness, and 3) Symbiosis as the goal. Conclusion: The study demonstrates that communication, situational awareness, and teamwork are closely interconnected non-technical skills that are central to collaboration between scrub nurses and circulating nurses. The findings suggest that sustained attentiveness, the ability to anticipate the development of events, and active listening contribute to the development of shared situational awareness and effective coordination of perioperative work. The study also highlights the importance of relational factors, with mutual trust and psychological safety emerging as essential prerequisites for open communication, collaboration, and the maintenance of patient safety. Future research should explore how collaboration between perioperative nurses is affected in settings with a greater proportion of emergency surgery, where the demands on non-technical skills may differ from those in elective surgical practice.

items.title: Toward an integrative theoretical model of AI-supported cybersecurity governance and organizational resilience
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports cybersecurity work through risk scoring, anomaly detection, alert triage, vulnerability prioritization, threat-intelligence enrichment, and incident-response assistance. Existing research explains important aspects of technical performance, responsible AI, cybersecurity oversight, and organizational decision-making, but it still provides limited explanation of how AI-generated analytical outputs become admissible, reviewable, and actionable within formal cybersecurity decision processes. This conceptual article develops the construct of AI-supported decision structures: the organizational arrangements through which AI-generated cybersecurity inputs are assessed for reliability and context, governed through use rules and escalation paths, embedded in recurring governance routines, connected to accountable decision ownership, and subjected to substantive human oversight. The article differentiates this construct from adjacent concepts in IS governance, AI governance, algorithmic management, human oversight, and digital surveillance governance. It also introduces theoretical tension by showing that stronger governance structures may improve decision quality and legitimacy while also creating trade-offs such as slower response, procedural overload, surveillance expansion, and symbolic compliance. The article develops a conceptual model and five mechanism-based propositions linking AI-supported decision structures to cybersecurity decision quality, decision legitimacy, coordinated response, and organizational resilience understood through anticipation, coping, and adaptation. The contribution is integrative rather than a claim of complete novelty: the framework recontextualizes established governance ideas around a distinct object of governance, namely AI-generated analytical inputs that shape cybersecurity judgment before formal authority is exercised.

items.title: Toward Culturalized Generative AI for the Creative and Cultural Industries: Lessons from Adaptive Cultural Mediation
items.abstract: This paper argues that contemporary generative AI systems are not yet consistently equipped to provide the level of culturalization required in the creative and cultural industries (CCIs). Debates on generative AI in cultural domains have focused primarily on productivity, innovation, intellectual property, labor disruption and bias. While these concerns are important, they do not fully capture a more basic issue: cultural production depends on forms of meaning that are historically situated, socially mediated and unevenly distributed across languages, communities and markets. In such contexts, fluency, safety and technical usefulness are not sufficient measures of system quality. The paper discusses how an existing line of thought from localization, cross-cultural design and culturalization research should be carried into the era of generative AI as explicit attention to cultural context, symbolic meaning and interpretive plurality. The CCIs provide a particularly revealing testbed for this claim because they expose limitations of generic AI evaluation in domains where value depends on tone, memory, symbolism and representation. The argument combines published evidence on cultural bias and uneven representation in contemporary models with diagnostic case studies using ChatGPT 5.5 in museums, heritage sites and pilgrimage contexts. These studies illustrate concrete cultural-mediation problems under the conditions tested. On that basis, the article proposes a framework for culturalized generative AI and outlines an integrated research and governance agenda spanning AI, the humanities and cultural-sector practice.

items.title: Toward precision hernia surgery: integrating biomarkers, genomics, quantitative imaging, and artificial intelligence in abdominal wall repair
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Despite technical advances, the expansion of minimally invasive approaches and the development of novel biomaterials, recurrence and complications following abdominal wall hernia (AWH) repair remain frequent. This variability likely reflects anatomical and technical factors and host biological heterogeneity. Precision herniology is emerging as a translational paradigm integrating biomarkers, genetics, quantitative imaging, and artificial intelligence to refine risk stratification and therapeutic planning. Methods We conducted a critical narrative review with translational scope. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from January 2015 to June 2026. We prioritized adult studies across four axes: (i) biomarkers of collagen, extracellular matrix, and cellular mechanisms; (ii) genetics and susceptibility to AWH; (iii) immunonutritional markers; (iv) artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for predicting complexity and complications. Results The literature reveals convergent, albeit heterogeneous, signals indicating that host biology may contribute to variability in hernia phenotype and surgical outcomes. Alterations in collagen turnover and in the MMP-TIMP axis, fibroblast heterogeneity, inflammatory signaling, polygenic architecture related to connective tissue integrity, immunonutritional markers associated with perioperative vulnerability, and quantitative imaging metrics analyzed by AI/ML models represent biologically plausible, clinically relevant domains. Conclusion Available data support the plausibility that host biological heterogeneity contributes to the formation, healing, prosthetic integration, and recurrence of AWH, thereby broadening the traditional paradigm centered predominantly on defect anatomy. The main value of this work is the critical integration of molecular and cellular biomarkers, genetics, quantitative imaging, and AI/ML into a unified conceptual framework for future precision herniology research.
